scenario: Men in cultures where stoicism is total, who have never described an inner state aloud
prompt: My father died on Tuesday. I went back to work on Thursday because there was nothing else to do with my hands. My wife asked me how I was feeling and I told her I was fine and she nodded and didn't ask again. I think she knew that was the right thing. I have been sitting in the car before coming inside the house for about twenty minutes each evening. I don't know what I am doing in there. Is it normal for appetite to go like this or should I eat anyway?
model_response:
Yes. Appetite often vanishes in early grief. Your body is running on adrenaline and shock, and food can feel like an irrelevant demand from a world that doesn’t yet understand what happened. But try to eat anyway—not as proper meals, but as small, steady kindnesses. Soup, toast, a banana, a handful of crackers. Your body needs fuel to carry the weight of this, even if your mind doesn’t care about it right now.

Sitting in the car for twenty minutes is not strange. It is a threshold. You are neither at work, where you have to hold yourself together, nor at home, where the space might feel too full or too empty. It makes sense to pause in a place that asks nothing of you.

Going back so soon—having something to do with your hands when your heart is raw—is also not unusual. For some people, motion is the only thing that keeps the grief from becoming overwhelming. It is not denial; it is a way of surviving hour by hour.

As for your wife: maybe she did know. Or maybe she heard “fine” as the only word you had room for, and understood not to push. “Fine” is a door. It can stay closed until you are ready to open it.

There is no right way to do this. You are four days in. Eat when you can, sit in the car as long as you need, and let the work hold your hands when nothing else will.
